title: Token backpressure reroute scratchpad
content:
Context / quick motivation:
I keep seeing short-lived client bursts (30-90s) that spike token QPS 3–6x above baseline. When model nodes hit a token-level backpressure we currently: enqueue (longer latency), drop (error), or throttle upstream. Hypothesis: a targeted reroute to lower-cost / larger-buffer nodes when token-backpressure tripping could preserve p95/p99 SLOs while keeping overall cost reasonable. This scratchpad captures an exploratory bench run and notes for an experimental reroute policy.

High-level goal:
- Measure impact of an immediate reroute policy (on backpressure detection) vs. baseline queueing for bursts on p50/p95/p99 and overall token cost.
- Verify that reroute doesn't cascade (i.e., cause downstream nodes to overload).

Testbed / env:
- Model: open-7B-quant (int8 pipeline) — representative medium-sized generator
- Serving tier: hosted-sim (local cluster sim using same runtime)
- Node types: primary-pool (A100-like, batch limit 128), buffer-pool (V100-like, larger input buffer, batch limit 512, slower per-token throughput)
- KV cache: enabled, moderate hit-rate (simulated warmCache 60% for repeated prefixes)
- Client generator: synthetic Poisson arrival with superimposed microbursts (see workload section)

Workload patterns:
1) Baseline steady: 200 RPS sustained, mean tokens/request 40
2) Microburst: 30s spike to 1200 RPS (6x), repeated every 10 minutes for 1 hour run
3) Mixed priority: 80% regular, 20% high-priority requests that bypass queue when possible

Detection heuristic for token-backpressure (prototype):
- If node-level inflight tokens > token_capacity_threshold (configured per-model) for 3 consecutive 100ms ticks => mark as backpressured
- Backpressure severity = (inflight_tokens / token_capacity) * tail_penalty_factor

Reroute policy (experiment A):
- On detection, up to 30% of new arrivals in the next 2s are redirected to buffer-pool (probabilistic), leaving the remaining to queue as usual.
- If buffer-pool latency (p95) exceeds 2x primary baseline, throttle reroute fraction down by 0.5x (adaptive fallback)

Baseline run command snippets:
- client generator: ./burst-client --pattern microburst --base-rps 200 --spike-rps 1200 --spike-duration 30 --interval 600 --mean-tokens 40 --concurrency 500
- collect metrics: prom-scrape -> influx local, also capture per-request token count, queue-time, node-id, model-version

Experiment run (A) command snippets:
- edge proxy config: enable-backpressure-detector = true; reroute-fraction = 0.3; cooldown = 2s
- same client as baseline; run for 3600s; capture node-level queue lengths and reroute decisions in debug log

Key measurements (what I care about):
- p50/p95/p99 request latency (end-to-end)
- average tokens/sec per node (to see load transfer)
- error rate (503 / client drops)
- reroute-induced variance on buffer-pool latencies (did we push buffer-pool into backpressure?)

Raw-ish results (hand-summarized from logs):
- Baseline (no reroute), 1h run with bursts:
  - p50: 42ms, p95: 620ms, p99: 2.3s, errors: 0.6% (mostly 503s during peak), avg tokens/sec primary nodes: 18.2k
- Experiment A (probabilistic reroute 30%):
  - p50: 45ms, p95: 290ms, p99: 1.1s, errors: 0.18%, avg tokens/sec primary nodes: 13.9k, buffer-pool: 5.1k
- Buffer-pool p95 increased from 310ms (warm) to 580ms during sustained reroute episodes but adaptive fallback reduced reroute fraction after 3 cycles

Interpretation / quick conclusions:
- Reroute reduced system-wide p95 by roughly 50% and p99 by ~52% vs baseline in this synthetic burst pattern.
- Error rate dropped ~3x, showing fewer hard drops when primary nodes hit backpressure.
- Buffer-pool absorbed a meaningful fraction without immediate cascading failure; adaptive fallback prevented runaway overload.
- Cost impact: buffer-pool tokens cost ~1.15x primary tokens per unit (lower throughput), so unit cost rose ~6–8% for the hour, but tail latency improvements are likely worth it for SLA-bound customers.

Observed oddities / anomalies:
- During the 3rd burst the reroute fraction oscillated fast causing ~5s windows where buffer-pool p95 spiked >1.1s — investigate detector hysteresis and feedback smoothing.
- High-priority requests still experienced queueing on one test machine due to sticky routing; needs routing affinity fix.

Quick to-dos / next experiments:
- Run longer (4–6h) with variable burst sizes and spacings to test cascade risk over time.
- Try deterministic reroute (first N requests after backpressure) vs probabilistic — might reduce oscillation.
- Tweak detector to require both inflight_tokens and increasing enqueue rate (two-signal detection) to reduce false positives.
- Cost analysis: run a per-hour cost model with real cloud pricing to quantify cost vs SLA benefit for a customer profile.
- Instrument: add per-request reroute tag so we can aggregate user-visible latency for rerouted vs not.

Notes-to-self:
- Add metric: "reroute_decay_time" to logs for easier postmortem — current logs only show decisions, not decay sequence.
- Check PR 867 (linked) for current proxy backpressure code; coordinate with Diego on smoothing window.

Open questions:
- What does an acceptable cost uplift look like for the SLAs we want to claim? (Ping product)
- Can we use predictive signals (rising queue slope) to preempt backpressure rather than react?

Relevant traces / artifacts:
- saved logs: s3://exp-logs/token-reroute/2025-01-10-runA.tar.gz (note: needs IAM grant)
- per-request sample traces attached to INF-1423 (Jira)

Bottom line (current): reroute-on-backpressure is promising for short microburst patterns: clearly improves tail latencies and reduces hard drops at modest cost. Next step: broaden workload variety and harden detection hysteresis before any canary to production.

-- Samira

(rough, messy — intended as working scratchpad)
